entwurf.beschreibung: JetBlue Airways, founded in 1999 and launched in 2000, combined low fares with in‑flight entertainment, kept profit after 9/11, cut seats in 2005 to save fuel, and formed a 2007 partnership with Aer Lingus.

teile.name: Part 1
teile.text: JetBlue launched flights on February eleven 2000, offering low fares, seat‑back televisions and SiriusXM satellite radio, a rare mix for U.S. carriers then.
teile.szene: An airport lounge buzzes with passengers watching in‑seat TVs, the JetBlue logo shining on a plane window, illustrating low‑cost travel with entertainment.
teile.bildtext: JetBlue launched in 2000, pioneering low‑cost travel with in‑seat entertainment and satellite radio services.

teile.name: Part 2
teile.text: The airline stayed profitable after 9/11, but fuel costs rose. So what did they change? In 2005 JetBlue removed a row of seats from each A320, lightening it by about nine hundred pounds and cut the crew from four to three.
teile.szene: A quiet boardroom, a CEO reviewing financial reports, with a skyline view of JFK, showcasing resilience in the early days of the post 9/11 era.
teile.bildtext: The airline gained profit during the 9/11 downturn, unlike most carriers by keeping operations.

teile.name: Part 3
teile.text: The February 2007 winter storm forced cancellations that cost roughly thirty million dollars and led JetBlue to partner with Aer Lingus for single‑ticket connections. Like, share, and save for more airline stories.
teile.szene: A maintenance hangar, technicians removing passenger seats from an Airbus, while engineers monitor fuel consumption on a digital screen today.
teile.bildtext: In 2005 JetBlue cut costs, removing seats to light planes and save fuel.
